articleTitle: Assessment of battery technologies for electric vehicles
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Systems for Electric Racing Vehicles
abstract: The duty cycle to which the battery in an all-electric racing vehicle is subjected is considerably more demanding than that of an urban electric vehicle. Indeed, the combination of high acceleration rates and full regenerative braking (which leads to high charge/discharge rates of the order of 20C) results in the need to operate well outside the limits recommended by the manufacturer. The author describes how, in order to accurately determine both the performance and the duration of a given power source an experimental facility has been constructed which enables a battery to be subjected to the same duty cycle as would be demanded by the race vehicle driven round a particular race circuit.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Project Volta-towards an electric speed record
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Systems for Electric Racing Vehicles
abstract: The authors present an overview of Project Volta, an attempt on an electric vehicle land speed record. Speed record cars tend to be of very different design to their circuit racing counterparts. However, Project Volta has enabled the authors to make a subjective assessment of the current level of European technology for all high speed electric propulsion. Although electric cars require particular design to account for their unusual weight/load distribution, they might be viewed in terms of existing race formulae.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Performance predictions for a single seater junior formula electric racing car
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Systems for Electric Racing Vehicles
abstract: The authors describe how the establishment of the range available for a high performance electric racing vehicle when it is at the design stage is a major factor in deciding the basic vehicle configuration, i.e. the battery type, battery mass vehicle aerodynamic drag characteristics, mass, motor size etc. In order to produce realistic range calculations, the simulation should, as far as possible, use data relating to actual circuit characteristics. It is thus desirable that the circuit simulation should reflect the anticipated usage for the electric racing vehicle. Data was therefore recorded for a Formula Vauxhall Junior single seater racing car on the Donnington Park Grand Prix circuit.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An advanced drive-train for electric racing vehicles
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Systems for Electric Racing Vehicles
abstract: The authors describe work carried out on the drive system for a battery-powered 4-wheel drive racing car, having a projected performance level approximately equivalent to that of a current Formula 3 vehicle and an overall weight of 1000 kg. The drive-train is optimised for a high system efficiency and low mass, and incorporates full regenerative braking in order to achieve the maximum running time.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A hybrid battery powered drivetrain for a high performance electric vehicle
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Systems for Electric Racing Vehicles
abstract: Electric racing vehicles tend to be either short range racers, using high specific performance starter type batteries, or long range endurance vehicles, using deep cycling slow discharge batteries. Whilst these are interesting exercises they have little relevance to what would be needed from a production electric vehicle. The aim of this paper is to define a possible electric sports saloon car with equivalent performance to a Rover Metro GTi.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The electric vehicle in motor sport-overview
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Systems for Electric Racing Vehicles
abstract: The author presents an overview of the electric vehicle motor sporting scene by covering the following topics: the extent of EV sporting activity worldwide; environmental considerations; sporting regulations; participating vehicles; and future prospects.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Influence of electric vehicle racing formulae on electric competition vehicle systems
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Systems for Electric Racing Vehicles
abstract: Electric vehicles (EV) racing formulae can be defined as any combination of parameters that affect the performance of EVs in competition, whether it be racing, record breaking or events of endurance, deviced by the organisers or governing bodies of such sporting events. Formulae for EV racing are usually based on overall vehicle weight, and whether the vehicle is road licensed or just a purpose-built special. Here, the author examines the influence of such electric vehicle racing formulae on the construction of electric competition vehicle systems.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Systems for Electric Racing Vehicles
abstract: A major objective in the design of vehicle propulsion systems is to maximise the power to weight ratio and hence performance, in particular, acceleration. With increasing concern for the environment, a requirement for energy efficiency and pollution abatement is being overlaid on performance targets, often leading to conflicting objectives. Here, the author describes how with modern developments in electric vehicle technology, such conflicts can be resolved through the optimal design of the primary power source and energy storage facility.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The history of the Electrathon (electric vehicle racing)
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Systems for Electric Racing Vehicles
abstract: In 1979 Lucas threw out a challenge to inventors-'how far can you travel using two Lucas car batteries as the only source of power'? The challenge was taken up enthusiastically by 52 contestants and the Lucas Electrathon was born. Here, the author gives an historical overview of the event, arguing that such competitive events, 'racing' in other circles, does improve the electric vehicle breed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
